questions.stem: Data were collected on 100 stamps from around the world. Two variables were primary color and width of stamp. Are these variables categorical or quantitative?
questions.answer_text: Primary color is categorical (it takes values that are names), and width is quantitative (it takes values that can be measured).

questions.stem: An elevator manufacturing company rates each elevator type with two variables: maximum number of passengers and maximum weight. Are these variables discrete or continuous?
questions.answer_text: Number of passengers is an integer, a countable variable, thus is discrete. Weight can take on an infinite number of values between any two values, thus is continuous.

questions.stem: Suppose that a study was carried out in which each student in a random sample of students at a particular high school was asked whether he or she thought too much homework was assigned in most classes. Which of the following is a correct understanding of the type of investigative question this study might address?
questions.answer_text: The data are categorical because each student responds yes or no. This leads to estimating a population proportion, that is, the proportion of students who feel that too much homework is assigned in most classes.

questions.stem: The times, in minutes, taken by 155 high school students to complete a level of the video game Angry Birds are summarized in the histogram below. Based on the histogram, which of the following must be true?
questions.answer_text: The minimum time is somewhere between 5 and 10 minutes but might not be exactly 5 minutes. Similarly, the maximum time is somewhere between 30 and 35 minutes. With 155 times, the middle time will be the 78th time if the times are arranged in order. There are 70 times less than 15 minutes and 40 times between 15 and 20 minutes, so the 78th time must be between 15 and 20 minutes.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a true statement?
questions.answer_text: Stemplots are not used for categorical data sets, are too unwieldy to be used for very large data sets, and show every individual value. Stems should never be skipped over—gaps are important to see.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an incorrect statement?
questions.answer_text: Histograms give information about relative frequencies (relative areas correspond to relative frequencies) and may or may not have an axis with actual frequencies. Symmetric histograms can have any number of peaks. Choice of width and number of classes changes the appearance of a histogram. Stemplots clearly show outliers; however, in histograms outliers may be hidden in large class widths.

questions.stem: In a favorite movie survey of 20 AP Statistics students, 4 chose Comedy, 5 chose Action, 6 chose Romance, 1 chose Drama, and 4 chose Sci-Fi. These data are illustrated in the following pie chart. Among those not choosing Comedy or Romance, what proportion chose Sci-Fi or Action?
questions.answer_text: The number of students not choosing Comedy or Romance was 20 − (4 + 6) or 5 + 1 + 4. Of these, 4 + 5 chose Sci-Fi or Action for a proportion of .

questions.stem: The miles run by 25 randomly selected runners during a given week are given below. Miles run 5 ≤ x < 10 10 ≤ x < 15 ≤ x < 20 ≤ x < (x) 15 20 25 Frequency 3 11 7 4 (a) Which is more appropriate for displaying these data, a dotplot, a stemplot, or a histogram? Explain. (b) What percent of the runners ran under 15 miles? (c) If each of the four intervals is divided in half and the corresponding numbers given, what percent would be under 15 miles?
questions.answer_text: (a) Given numerical data and four bins with corresponding frequencies immediately leads to the construction of a histogram. Dotplots and stemplots cannot be constructed when individual values are unknown. (b) (c) The answer would still be 56%.

questions.stem: The dotplot below shows the numbers of goals scored by the 20 teams playing in a city’s high school soccer games on a particular day. (a) Describe the distribution. (b) One superstar scored six goals, but his team still lost. What are all possible final scores for that game? Explain. (c) Is it possible that each of the teams that scored exactly two goals were the winners of that game? Explain.
questions.answer_text: (a) A complete answer mentions shape, center, spread, and unusual features (such as outliers) while including context within the description. Shape: Unimodal, skewed right, probable outlier at 10. Center: Around 2 or 3. Spread: From 0 to 10 goals were scored by each team. (b) If the player scored six goals on his own, then his/her team must have scored either 7 or 10 goals. Since the team lost, the only possible final score is 10 to 7. (c) No, there were six teams that scored exactly two goals, but there were only five teams that scored less than two goals. So, not all the two-goal teams could have won.

questions.stem: The winning percentages for a major league baseball team over the past 22 years are shown in the following stemplot: (a) Interpret the lowest value. (b) Describe the distribution. (c) Give a reason that one might argue that the team is more likely to lose a given game than win it. (d) Give a reason that one might argue that the team is more likely to win a given game than lose it.
questions.answer_text: (a) The lowest winning percentage over the past 22 years was 46.0%. (b) A complete answer mentions shape, center, spread, and unusual features (such as outliers) while including context within the description. Shape: Two clusters, each somewhat bell-shaped. Center: Around 50%. Spread: The winning percentages were between 46.0% and 55.6%. (c) The team had more losing seasons (13) than winning seasons (9). (d) The cluster of winning percentages is further away from 50% than the cluster of losing percentages.

questions.stem: Data collected from over 10,000 graduating college seniors asked about economic backgrounds and leadership position experiences. The data are summarized in the following table: Economic background Medium Lower income income Higher income Number of students 1,450 8,280 2,975 Number claiming leadership role 377 2,760 1,428 (a) What is the investigative question of interest? (b) Are the data categorical or numerical? Explain. (c) Explain why a relative frequency distribution is more appropriate than a frequency distribution in analyzing the data. (d) The following bar chart is constructed from the data. What does it indicate about the relationship between college students’ economic backgrounds and leadership position experience?
questions.answer_text: (a) Is there a relationship between college students’ economic backgrounds and leadership position experience? (b) Categorical, taking on values that are categories (economic background). (c) Relative frequencies are more appropriate in analyzing these data because there are different numbers of students who were surveyed from each economic category. (d) Students who enter college with certain advantages seem to accrue additional advantages in college. In this survey, higher-income economic backgrounds were associated with higher levels of leadership position experience.

questions.stem: Many students perceive e-cigarettes as less harmful than traditional cigarettes, but research shows that both cigarettes and e-cigarettes can lead to nicotine addiction, respiratory issues, and other health problems. Data collected from over 5,000 students asking about e- cigarette use are summarized in the following table. Current school level Middle school High school College Number of students 1,400 2,900 1,800 Number admitting to using e- 51 241 371 cigarettes (a) What is the investigative question of interest? (b) Are the data categorical or numerical? Explain. (c) Explain why a relative frequency distribution is more appropriate than a frequency distribution in analyzing the data. (d) The following bar chart showing relative frequencies of e- cigarette use by school level is constructed from the data. What does the bar chart indicate about the relationship between school level and e-cigarette use?
questions.answer_text: (a) Is there convincing statistical evidence of a relationship between school level and e-cigarette use in the population of all students in middle school, high school, and college? (b) Categorical, because the data are counts. (c) Relative frequencies are more appropriate in analyzing these data because there are different numbers of students who were surveyed from each school level. (d) Middle school students have the lowest relative frequency use of e-cigarettes. High school students appear to have a relative frequency use of e-cigarettes more than double that of middle school students. College students appear to have a relative frequency use of e- cigarettes more than double that of high school students. In this survey, higher e-cigarette use was associated with higher school levels.

questions.stem: A medical researcher performs a year-long test to compare two new weight loss medications. Each of 46 volunteers takes Medication A for 6 months and Medication B for 6 months. Twenty-three of the participants are randomly chosen to take A first while the remaining 23 participants take B first. The difference in weight loss (under Medication A minus under Medication B) for the participants is summarized in the following stemplot. (a) Explain what a negative difference indicates in the context of this study. (b) Describe the distribution given by the stemplot. (c) What conclusion is reasonable from this set of data? Explain.
questions.answer_text: (a) A negative difference indicates a volunteer who lost more weight taking Medication B than taking Medication A. (b) The distribution of differences in weight loss (under Medication A minus under Medication B) is skewed left (toward lower values), has a center around 3.1 pounds, and has a range of 8.5 − (−5.0) = 13.5 pounds. (c) Medication A appears to be more effective for weight loss. Eleven participants lost more weight with Medication B, while 35 participants lost more weight with Medication A.

questions.answer_text: Multiplying every value in a set by the same constant (in this case, by ) multiplies both the mean and the standard deviation by the same constant. Standardized scores (the number of standard deviations from the mean) are unchanged and without units.

Summary statistics are noted below: Min = 10 Max = 60 First quartile Third quartile = 25 = 38 Median = 31 Mean = 31.4 n = 55 s = 11.6 Which of the following is a true statement?
questions.answer_text: Outliers are any values below Q1 − 1.5(IQR) = 25 − 1.5(38 − 25) = 5.5 or above Q3 + 1.5(IQR) = 38 + 1.5(38 − 25) = 57.5. With a minimum of 10 > 5.5, there are no outliers on the low end; however, with a maximum of 60 > 57.5, the maximum is an outlier and so are any other values falling between 57.5 and 60.

questions.stem: Victims spend from 5 to 5,840 hours repairing the damage caused by identity theft with a mean of 330 hours and a standard deviation of 245 hours. (a) What would be the mean, range, standard deviation, and variance for hours spent repairing the damage caused by identity theft if each of the victims spent an additional 10 hours? (b) What would be the mean, range, standard deviation, and variance for hours spent repairing the damage caused by identity theft if each of the victims’ hours spent increased by 10%?
questions.answer_text: (a) Adding 10 to each value increases the mean by 10 but leaves measures of variability unchanged. So, the new mean is 340 hours while the range stays at 5,835 hours, the standard deviation remains at 245 hours, and the variance remains at 2452 = 60,025 hr2. (b) Increasing each value by 10% (multiplying by 1.10) will increase the mean to 1.1(330) = 363 hours, the range to 1.1(5,835) = 6,418.5 hours, the standard deviation to 1.1(245) = 269.5 hours, and the variance to (269.5)2 = 72,630.25 hr2. (Note that the variance increases by a multiple of (1.1)2 and not by a multiple of 1.1.)

questions.stem: Are women better than men at multitasking? Suppose in one study of multitasking a random sample of 200 female and 200 male high school students were assigned several tasks at the same time, such as solving simple mathematics problems, reading maps, and answering simple questions while talking on a telephone. Total times taken to complete all the tasks are given in the histograms below. Write a few sentences comparing the distributions of times to complete all tasks by females and by males.
questions.answer_text: A complete answer compares shape, center, and spread and mentions context in at least one of the responses. Shape: The distribution of times to complete all tasks by females is skewed right (toward the higher values), whereas the distributions of times to complete all tasks by males is roughly bell-shaped. Center: The center of the distribution of female times (at around minutes) is less than the center of the distribution of male times (at around minutes). Spread: The spreads of the two distributions are roughly the same; the range of the female times ( minutes) equals the range of the male times ( minutes).

questions.stem: Suppose a distribution has mean 300 and standard deviation 25. If the z-score of Q1 is −0.7 and the z-score of Q3 is 0.7, what values would be considered outliers?
questions.answer_text: z-scores give the number of standard deviations from the mean, so Q1 = 300 − 0.7(25) = 282.5 and Q3 = 300 + 0.7(25) = 317.5. The interquartile range is IQR = 317.5 − 282.5 = 35, and 1.5(IQR) = 1.5(35) = 52.5. The standard definition of outliers encompasses all values less than Q1 − 52.5 = 230 and all values greater than Q3 + 52.5 = 370.

questions.stem: Below are population pyramids from Liberia and Canada. (a) The approximate median age of the Liberian population falls in which of these intervals: 0–4, 15–19, 30–34, 40–44? Explain. (b) Explain why it is impossible to calculate the mean age of either population. (c) Which country has more children younger than 10 years of age? Explain. (d) Does the population pyramid indicate that Canadian men or Canadian women live longer? Explain. (e) In 2010, Liberia had recently come out of a civil war with the extensive use of child soldiers. How is this visible in the population pyramid?
questions.answer_text: (a) The Liberian median age lies in the 15–19 age interval because roughly 50% of the total bar lengths is above and below the 15–19 interval. (b) Numerical values are needed to calculate means. Histograms such as these give numbers or proportions of values in specific intervals but do not give the actual values. (c) Canada has more children younger than 10 years of age. There are about 1.2 million children younger than age 10 in Liberia (boys and girls) and roughly 3.5 million in Canada. (Note the difference in scales!) (d) The population pyramid indicates that Canadian women live longer than men because all the higher age intervals show greater numbers of women than men. (e) In the Liberian graph, the smaller 15–19 age group shows a definite break with the overall pattern. A plausible explanation is that a great number of children died in the civil war.

questions.stem: An entrepreneur owns two restaurants, one advertised as casual dining and the other advertised as fine dining. To estimate time spent in his restaurants, the entrepreneur randomly samples 42 customers, 14 with reservations at the casual dining site and 28 with reservations at the fine dining site. (a) Compare the two distributions of dining times. (b) How many of the dining times were under 90 minutes? (c) Based on the histograms, what is a reasonable estimate for the median dining time for this random sample of 42 customers?
questions.answer_text: (a) The distribution of casual dining times is roughly right skewed, while the distribution of fine dining times is roughly bell-shaped. Both the center and the spread are greater for the fine dining times. (b) There were 12 + 3 = 15 dining times under 90 minutes. (c) All 14 casual dining times were under 105 minutes as were 5 of the fine dining times. A total of 19 dining times were under 105 minutes, and a total of 19 + 4 = 23 were under 120 minutes. With a total of 42 dining times, the median is between the 21st and 22nd times, so it must be somewhere between 105 and 120 minutes.

(c) There were 4 + 10 = 14 first serves under 118 mph and 11 + 3 = 14 first serves over 118. The median first serve speed among the 30 players was 118 mph.

questions.stem: A sports statistician plans to survey Division 1 college football programs as to graduation rates of their student athletes. The statistician will use a cluster random sample with the NCAA Division 1 football conferences as clusters. A random sample of two conferences will be selected and their football programs analyzed. What is one disadvantage to selecting a cluster random sample to investigate Division 1 football program graduation rates?
questions.answer_text: Cluster random samples work when each cluster roughly looks like the population as a whole. However, there is no reason to believe that each conference has similar graduation rates as any other conference. Some conferences may have different academic standards and different support levels for their student athletes. Picking two conferences may not at all be representative of the population of Division 1 college football programs. In general, cluster random samples are known for ease, convenience, and less expense than other sampling methods. Homogeneity among schools in given conferences would relate to picking a stratified random sample with the conferences as strata.

questions.stem: Political advisors want to survey registered voters as to their top concerns. Which of the following sampling methods does NOT have voluntary response bias as a potential source of error? In each case, assume all 100 chosen people answer the survey.
questions.answer_text: Voluntary response bias results from surveys based on individuals who choose to participate. Examples include when people choose to call in to a radio station, to respond to a newspaper ad, to approach and answer a surveyor’s questions, or to respond to an online website. The example in which people are randomly chosen from a voter registration list and all answer a survey would not involve voluntary response bias.

questions.stem: A survey is to be taken as to whether or not people believe the moon landing conspiracy theory, which claims the six crewed landings (1969–1972) were faked. Which of the following describes a design in which nonresponse bias is likely present?
questions.answer_text: Nonresponse bias is a potential problem whenever a survey does not obtain responses from everyone surveyed. Choice (A) has potential voluntary response bias, and choice (D) has potential undercoverage bias. However, choices (A), (C), and (D) all achieved responses from everyone who was surveyed, so they do not have nonresponse bias.

questions.stem: A student is interested in estimating the average length of words in a 600-page textbook and plans the following three-stage sampling procedure: I. After noting that each of the 12 chapters has a different author, the student decides to obtain a sample of words from each chapter. II. Each chapter is approximately 50 pages long. The student uses a random number generator to pick three pages from each chapter and use all words from these pages to find the average length of words for that author. III. On each chosen page, the student notes the length of every tenth word. (a) The first stage above represents what kind of sampling procedure? Give an advantage in using it in this context. (b) The second stage above represents what kind of sampling procedure? Give an advantage in using it in this context. (c) The third stage above represents what kind of sampling procedure? Give a disadvantage to using it dependent upon an author’s writing style.
questions.answer_text: (a) This is an example of stratified random sampling, where the chapters are strata. The advantage is that the student is ensuring that the final sample will represent the 12 different authors, who may well use different average word lengths. (b) This is an example of cluster random sampling, where for each chapter the three chosen pages are clusters. It is reasonable to assume that each page (cluster) resembles the author’s overall pattern. The advantage is that using these clusters is much more practical than trying to sample from among all an author’s words. (c) This is an example of systematic random sampling, which is quicker and easier than many other procedures. A possible disadvantage is that if ordering is related to the variable under consideration, this procedure will likely result in an unrepresentative sample. For example, in this study if an author’s word length is related to word order in sentences, the student could end up with words of particular lengths.

questions.stem: Pelicans are considered an endangered species, and there is a need to protect them from becoming extinct. Unfortunately, the U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service is unable to protect all pelican colonies; however, it plans to protect those colonies identified as most important. One criterion in determining the importance of a geographical region is the density of nesting sites within it. Given an aerial view of the nests in a geographical region used for pelican nesting, the service plans to divide the rectangular picture into 150 equal-size plots as below: The service will randomly pick 15 plots (10% of the total), count the nests in each of those plots, sum and multiply by 10 to estimate the total number of nests in the region, and then calculate density. Two methods for counting the number of nests are under consideration. Method I: Randomly pick one of the above rows and use all the 15 plots in that row. Method II: Randomly pick one of the plots in each of the 15 columns to obtain the 15 plots. (a) What sampling procedure is each method striving for, and how can each method be implemented? (b) Which of these two methods is preferable here? Explain.
questions.answer_text: (a) Method I results in cluster random sampling (the rows are clusters) and can be implemented by numbering the rows 1 through 10, using a random number generator to randomly pick a number between 1 and 10, and using all 15 plots in that row. Method II results in stratified random sampling (the columns are strata) and can be implemented by numbering the rows 1 through 10, using a random number generator to pick a number between 1 and 10 to pick a plot in the first column, repeating this process to pick a random plot in each of the 15 columns, and using the 15 plots resulting from picking one plot from each column. (b) Method II, a stratified random sample (with the columns as strata), would be preferable here as each column is somewhat different, so picking a plot from each is meaningful. Method I, an attempt at cluster random sampling with the rows as clusters, would work only if each of the rows was heterogeneous (representative of the whole area); this is clearly not true as, for example, the top and bottom rows have far fewer nests than the middle rows.

questions.stem: For each of the following survey designs, identify the problem and the effect it would have on the estimate of interest. (a) Should spending be increased for the athletic program? A school official decides to sample spectators randomly at the next home basketball game. (b) Do people believe that eating organic will lower the risk of cancer? A health magazine sends a questionnaire to all their subscribers. (c) A supermarket quality control inspector opens boxes of strawberries. If no mold is seen among the visible strawberries, he accepts the box. (d) Are the patients following their diet instructions? A family physician asks each of her patients during their office visits. (e) Parents are asked to write to a newspaper with a yes or no response to whether or not they are happy with the education their children are receiving in the local public schools.
questions.answer_text: (a) People who attend the school’s basketball game are probably more interested in supporting the athletic program than those who do not attend. This study will probably show that a higher proportion of people favor the increased spending than what is the true proportion. (b) Subscribers to a health magazine are more likely to believe in the benefits of eating organic than the general population, so the resulting proportion of believers in this study will be greater than it is in the general population. (c) The distributer could put any moldy strawberries on the bottom, out of sight! The proportion of accepted boxes will be higher than it should be. (d) Many patients will be reluctant to admit to their doctor that they are not following their diet instructions. So, the proportion who say they are following the instructions will be higher than the true proportion following the instructions. (e) Parents who are satisfied with the school system are probably less likely to take the time to respond to this voluntary response survey, while those who are unhappy with the education their kids are receiving are more likely to respond. So, the proportion of “unhappy” responses will probably be higher than the true proportion of parents who are unhappy.

questions.stem: Suppose we are trying to estimate the mean age of high school teachers and have four methods of choosing samples. We choose 10 samples using each method. Later we find the true mean, μ = 42. The following are plots of the results of each sampling method. (a) Which method or methods indicate high precision? Explain. (b) Which method or methods indicate probable bias? Explain.
questions.answer_text: (a) Methods A and C indicate high precision because they result in statistics that are tightly clustered. (b) Methods C and D indicate probable bias because they result in statistics that are not centered around the true population parameter. Note that shape and variability are irrelevant to the issue of bias. Bias is focused on the center of the distribution.

questions.stem: Air Quality Index (AQI) is the EPA’s index for reporting air quality. An AQI value of 50 or below represents good air quality, while an AQI value over 150 represents unhealthy air quality. Suppose that the distribution of AQI scores in the 500 highest-income counties is roughly normal with a mean of 50, while the distribution of AQI scores in the 500 lowest-income counties is roughly normal with a mean of 100. The figure below represents the distributions of AQI scores in these high- and low-income counties. For an environmental study, 110 of these 1,000 counties will be randomly selected. Two methods are under consideration. Method I: Take an SRS from among the 1,000 low- and high- income counties. Method II: Randomly select either the low- or high-income counties and take an SRS of those 500 counties. (a) Will a sample obtained using Method II be representative of the 1,000 counties? Explain. (b) Which of the two sampling methods will result in a sample with less variability in AQI? Explain. (c) The figure below represents the AQI of 110 counties obtained by using one of the two methods. Explain which method was most likely used.
questions.answer_text: (a) No, a sample obtained using Method II will not be representative of the 1,000 counties. It will only be representative of either the low- or the high-income counties, whichever was randomly chosen. (b) Method II will result in less variability in AQI because all the scores will come from the one randomly selected income group of 500 similar-income counties. (c) Method I was most likely used to select this sample. The bimodal shape of the sample distribution indicates that counties were likely selected from both high- and low-income groups, which happens with Method I. Method II would most likely result in a unimodal distribution centered around either 50 or 100.

options.B: Randomly select 5 teams out of the 50, and choose all 6 players from each of the 5 teams to participate in the survey.
options.C: Randomly pick 10 players from each of the 3 conferences to participate in the survey.
options.D: Number the players 1 through 300, and randomly pick a number between 1 and 10 to start with. Choose the corresponding player and every 10th player from that point forward to participate in the survey.

questions.stem: A sociologist plans to survey 30 college tennis players about whether or not they plan to turn pro at some point. On a randomly selected day, there were 50 teams participating, each with 6 players for a total of 300 players. The 50 teams come from 3 different conferences. Which of the following describes a cluster random sampling method?
questions.answer_text: Cluster random sampling involves dividing the population into heterogeneous groups called clusters and then picking everyone or everything in a random selection of one or more of the clusters. In this situation, the teams were the clusters. Choice (A) was an SRS, choice (C) was a stratified random sample with the conferences as strata, and choice (D) was a systematic random sample.

options.A: This was an observational study, and the response variable was the concentration of the contaminant.
options.B: This was an observational study, and the response variable was the distance from the dump site.
options.C: This was an experiment, and the response variable was the concentration of the contaminant.
options.D: This was an experiment, and the response variable was the distance from the dump site.

questions.stem: Five soil samples were taken within 50 feet of a dump site, and 5 more soil samples were taken over 100 feet away from the dump site. Measurements were taken of the concentration of a particularly dangerous contaminant. What type of study was conducted, and what was the response variable?
questions.answer_text: No treatment was applied, so this was an observational study, not an experiment. Measurements were taken of the concentration of the contaminant, so concentration was the response variable.

options.A: The survey question asked, “Do you feel employees are greedy and unrealistic with regard to overtime pay?”
options.B: Surveys were handed out to and completed by all the employees in the 8-to-5 work schedule.
options.C: Surveys were completed by a random sample taken of roughly 10% of the employee base.
options.D: Surveys were mailed to all employees, and 50% were returned.

questions.stem: A survey was designed to collect information about employees’ satisfaction with regard to overtime pay. Which of the following describes a procedure in which nonresponse bias is likely?
questions.answer_text: Nonresponse bias occurs when a substantial number of contacted people choose not to respond. People choosing to respond and people not choosing to respond might have very different opinions, which can lead to unreliable conclusions if only one group participates.

questions.stem: A company has 50 employees, 40 blue-collar workers and 10 white- collar workers, and all workers belong to a company union. The union plans to form a 5-person committee to represent the union in negotiations for a new contract. (a) For sake of convenience, the union is considering picking an SRS. Describe a process for choosing a simple random sample of 5 people from among the 50 employees. (b) An alternative sampling method would be to select a stratified random sample where the two strata are the blue-collar workers and the white-collar workers. In the context of this situation, give a statistical advantage of selecting a stratified random sample as opposed to an SRS.
questions.answer_text: (a) Number the employees 1 through 50. Use a random number generator to pick integers between 1 and 50, throwing out repeats, until 5 unique integers are picked. The committee will consist of the 5 employees with numbers corresponding to the 5 integers. (b) With stratified random sampling, you could guarantee both blue-collar and white-collar employees on the committee. With an SRS, you could end up with only blue-collar or only white-collar employees on the committee. This is important because blue-collar and white- collar employees might have different concerns with regard to the issues under negotiation.

questions.stem: Researchers performed a study to determine if increasing daily protein ingestion contributes to gaining lean body mass, muscle strength, and physical test performance in healthy student athletes at the college level. Thirty student athlete volunteers were randomly assigned to 3 groups, each group following the identical set diet. Each day for 5 weeks, participants in group 1 were given a supplement of 1 gram of protein per kilogram of body weight, participants in group 2 were given a supplement of 2 grams of protein per kilogram of body weight, and participants in group 3 received no protein supplement. (a) Was this an experiment or an observational study? Explain. (b) Why was a group included that received no supplement? (c) Is it reasonable to generalize conclusions from this study beyond the 30 participants? Explain.
questions.answer_text: (a) Treatments (supplemental protein) were applied, so this was an experiment. (b) The purpose of the experiment was to see if ingesting supplemental protein is more effective in gaining lean body mass, muscle strength, and physical test performance than ingesting no protein supplement. To do a comparison, there needed to be a group that received no supplement. The study also allows for investigating two different levels of supplemental protein. (c) These 30 student-athletes were volunteers, who may not represent the population of student- athletes. For example, the volunteers might be more interested in muscle mass and do more weight training than other student-athletes. Ingesting supplemental protein and weight training would then be confounded. So it is not reasonable to generalize conclusions from this study beyond the 30 participants.

questions.stem: A grocery store manager decides to do a survey to see if passing out a free piece of candy to the first 50 customers is more of an inducement to purchase candy than offering a storewide sale on candy. On a randomly chosen day, he surveys the first 100 customers who enter the store by asking the following question, “Some managers believe that customers arriving early at the store deserve a reward. Would you rather receive a free piece of candy for arriving early, or would you rather the store offer a storewide sale on candy?” (a) Explain how bias may have been introduced based on the way the convenience sample was selected, and suggest a way of selecting the sample to avoid this bias. (b) Explain how bias may have been introduced based on the way the question was worded, and explain how this bias could have been avoided.
questions.answer_text: (a) Surveying the first customers to arrive introduces undercoverage bias because the survey deals with offering a reward for early arrivals. A better method would be to choose a random sample from among all the customers shopping at that store because early arrivals and later arrivals will probably have different views on giving a reward to early arrivals. (b) Wording such as “deserve a reward” may lead early arrivals to say that is the alternative they prefer. It would be more neutral to simply ask, “Would you rather receive a free piece of candy for arriving early or would you rather the store offer a storewide sale on candy?”

questions.stem: There are approximately 1,800 public colleges and 4,000 private colleges in the United States. A survey is to be taken of the students of U.S. colleges, and two sampling methods have been proposed. Method I: Randomly select 25 colleges from among the 5,800 colleges, and survey all the students at those colleges. Method II: Randomly select 2,000 students from the public colleges and 4,500 students from the private colleges to survey. (a) Identify the method that results in a stratified random sample, and identify the strata. (b) Identify the method that results in a cluster random sample, and identify the clusters. (c) Give one statistical advantage and one statistical disadvantage of using Method I. (d) Give one statistical advantage and one statistical disadvantage of using Method II.
questions.answer_text: (a) Method II results in a stratified random sample where the students attending public colleges are one strata and the students attending private colleges are a second strata. (b) Method I results in a cluster random sample where the 5,800 colleges are the clusters. (c) An advantage of Method I (cluster random sampling) is that only 25 colleges need to be surveyed, while a disadvantage is that the students surveyed might be all or mostly from either the private colleges or the public colleges (undercoverage bias). (d) An advantage of Method II (stratified random sampling) is that it guarantees that students from both private and public colleges will be surveyed, while a disadvantage is that it necessitates listing a very large number of students from which to be able to pick randomly.

questions.stem: A large company is investigating ways of promoting greater productivity. Two programs they are considering are to provide at the beginning of the workday either short professional-led exercise sessions or short professional-led meditation sessions. One hundred employees volunteer to participate. Their productivity will be measured before and after a 2-month period of sessions. (a) Some of the volunteers who are friends ask to be placed into the same program. Give an example of why this would not be a good idea as far as measuring the success of one or the other program. (b) What advantage would there be to include a control group? (c) Will it be reasonable to generalize any conclusion from this study?
questions.answer_text: (a) If the friends are all in the same department and if something happened in the department to change productivity, this would be confounded with the program being implemented. (b) If something new occurred in the whole company that affected productivity, without the control group it would not be possible to know what increased productivity, one of the programs or what occurred in the whole company. (c) It would not be reasonable to generalize any conclusion because the study was with volunteers. People who volunteer might be more motivated and would increase productivity simply because they were being observed.

options.A: Random sampling
options.B: Random assignment
options.C: Control
options.D: Replication

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a primary element of experimental design?
questions.answer_text: Random sampling can be used in experimental design but is not a primary element like it is with observational studies.

options.A: Double-sided
options.B: Double-sample
options.C: Double-blind
options.D: Double-origin

questions.stem: Which name describes an experiment where neither the subjects nor the response evaluators know which subjects are in the treatment group and which are in the control group?
questions.answer_text: Double-blinding is often important so that those who measure responses are not influenced by the knowledge of which subjects are receiving which treatments.

options.A: Ambiguous effect
options.B: Mistaken effect
options.C: Placebo effect
options.D: Psychological effect

questions.stem: What is the name of the beneficial effect experienced by some patients due to the patients’ belief in the treatment?
questions.answer_text: The placebo effect refers to the fact that some people will respond to a perceived treatment even though their treatment is actually an inactive treatment—for example, receiving a sugar pill rather than a medication.

options.A: subjects; treatments
options.B: subjects; response variables
options.C: statistical significance; statistical confidence
options.D: explanatory variables; response variables

questions.stem: Randomized experiments allow for cause-and-effect conclusions between ____ and ____.
questions.answer_text: Experiments aim to discover whether a treatment of interest (explanatory variable) has a proposed effect (response variable).

options.A: Census
options.B: Sample survey
options.C: Experiment
options.D: Observational study

questions.stem: Suppose you wish to compare the average class size of mathematics classes to the average class size of English classes in your high school. Which is the most appropriate technique for gathering the needed data?
questions.answer_text: The main office at your school should be able to give you the class sizes of every math and English class. If need be, you can check with every math and English teacher.

options.A: Both studies are observational studies because of the time period involved.
options.B: Both studies are observational studies because there are no control groups.
options.C: The first study is an observational study, while the second is an experiment.
options.D: The first study is an experiment, while the second is an observational study.

questions.stem: Two studies are run to compare the experiences of families living in high-rise public housing to those of families living in townhouse subsidized rentals. The first study interviews 25 families who have been in each government program for at least 1 year, while the second randomly assigns 25 families to each program and interviews them after 1 year. Which of the following is a true statement?
questions.answer_text: In the first study, the families were already in the housing units, while in the second study, one of two treatments was applied to each family.

options.A: There are four explanatory variables and one response variable.
options.B: There is one explanatory variable with four levels of response.
options.C: Miles per gallon is the only explanatory variable, but there are four response variables corresponding to the different octanes.
options.D: There are four levels of a single explanatory variable.

questions.stem: A consumer product agency tests miles per gallon for a sample of automobiles using each of four different octanes of gasoline. Which of the following is true?
questions.answer_text: Octane is the only explanatory variable, and it is being tested at four levels. Miles per gallon is the single response variable.

options.A: Although this study indicates a relation, it does not prove causation.
options.B: There could well be a confounding variable responsible for the seeming relationship.
options.C: Self-selection here makes drawing the counselors’ conclusion difficult.
options.D: A more meaningful study would be to compare a simple random sample (SRS) from each of the two groups of 100 students.

questions.stem: A study is made to determine whether taking AP Statistics in high school helps students achieve higher GPAs when they go to college. In comparing records of 200 college students, half of whom took AP Statistics in high school, it is noted that the average college GPA is higher for those 100 students who took AP Statistics than for those who did not. Based on this study, guidance counselors begin recommending AP Statistics for college-bound students. Which of the following is incorrect?
questions.answer_text: Using only a sample from the observations gives less information. It may well be that very bright students are the same ones who both choose to take AP Statistics and have high college GPAs. If students could be randomly assigned to take or not take AP Statistics, the results would be more meaningful. Of course, ethical considerations might make it impossible to isolate the confounding variable in this way.

options.A: This was a randomized experiment, which gave strong evidence that regular exercise causes greater heart strength.
options.B: This was an observational study, which proved that regular exercise causes greater heart strength.
options.C: This was an observational study, which gave strong evidence that regular exercise causes greater heart strength.
options.D: It is likely that there is a confounding variable.

questions.stem: A cardiologist surveyed a random sample of adults aged 21 to 75, looking at whether or not they reported exercising regularly and then used an echocardiogram to measure heart strength of those surveyed. She found a strong positive association. Which of the following is a proper conclusion?
questions.answer_text: Association does not imply causation. It is likely that regular exercise and a person’s age are both associated with greater heart strength, and either one could be the cause of the greater heart strength. Regular exercise and age are confounded. An experiment in which people are randomly assigned to exercise or not can prove a causal relationship between exercise and heart strength.

options.A: to reduce bias.
options.B: to reduce variation.
options.C: as a substitute for a control group.
options.D: as a first step in randomization.

questions.stem: In designing an experiment, blocking is used
questions.answer_text: Blocking divides the subjects into groups, such as men and women, or political affiliations, and thus reduces variation. That is, when we group similar individuals together into blocks and then randomize within the blocks, much of the variability due to the differences between the blocks is accounted for and so comparison of the treatment groups is clearer.

questions.stem: For each of the following, would you recommend using random sampling, random assignment, both, or neither? Explain. (a) A movie critic wants to investigate whether a greater proportion of teenagers in public or private schools have seen all three of the Back to the Future films. (b) A company CEO wants to investigate whether giving hourly pay raises or end-of-the-year bonuses leads to greater productivity on an assembly line. (c) A sportscaster wants to investigate whether the Chicago Cubs or the Chicago White Sox won a greater number of interleague games during the shortened 2020 season.
questions.answer_text: (a) This cannot involve random assignment as it makes no sense to randomly assign teenagers to go to public or private schools. However, it would be good to use random sampling to select teenagers from each type of school to be asked about Back to the Future movies so as to be able to generalize to the population of public and private schools. (b) It is important for the company CEO to use random assignment to receive hourly pay raises or end-of-the-year bonuses because a cause-and-effect conclusion is of interest. (c) The sportscaster would probably want to include all the interleague games played by the Cubs and White Sox during the shortened 2020 season, and thus use neither random sampling nor random assignment.

questions.stem: Rock and pop fame is associated with risk-taking and premature mortality. A study following the lives of 100 rock and pop stars periodically asked them about their frequency of substance abuse and followed their lives until death. Researchers noted the age of death and noticed that a greater amount of substance abuse was associated with an earlier age at death. (a) What are the explanatory and response variables? (b) Is this a prospective observational study, a retrospective observational study, or an experiment? Explain. (c) Does this study show that greater frequency of substance abuse leads to early death?
questions.answer_text: (a) The explanatory variable is the frequency of substance abuse. The response variable is the age at death. (b) This is a prospective observational study. No treatments were assigned, and the researchers asked the rock and pop stars to report their frequency of substance abuse and later noted their ages at time of death. (c) No, this is an observational study, so no cause-and-effect conclusion is possible. It is possible that other variables are influencing the response. For example, rock and pop stars might engage in other forms of risk taking, such as poor eating and poor sleep patterns, which also might negatively affect life expectancy.

questions.stem: Much of the profit in movie theaters comes from sales at the concession stands. A theater manager wants to run an experiment to evaluate whether subliminal advertising will help to increase sales. He has software that flashes “BUY POPCORN” on the screen for a fraction of a second. (a) What are the explanatory and response variables? (b) Is this a prospective observational study, a retrospective observational study, or an experiment? Explain. (c) Should blinding and/or double-blinding or neither be incorporated? Explain. (d) Should random sampling or random assignment be incorporated? Explain how. (e) Why is it important to have some kind of control with regard to which days the subliminal message takes place? (f) In context, explain how a cause-and-effect conclusion will or will not be justified.
questions.answer_text: (a) The explanatory variable is flashing or not flashing “BUY POPCORN” on the screen for a fraction of a second. The response variable is the quantity of popcorn sold. (b) This is an experiment because a treatment, flashing “BUY POPCORN,” is performed on certain days. There is a control group, the days when no flashing takes place. (c) Double-blinding should be incorporated. It is important that customers don’t know they are seeing or not seeing the subliminal message as that knowledge might influence whether or not they buy popcorn. It is also important that the clerks selling the popcorn don’t know which days the message will be flashing as that might impact how they react to customers. (d) Random assignment should be incorporated. For example, every day for some specified period of time, the manager could flip a coin. If heads, flash the subliminal message all day on the screen. If tails, though, don’t flash the message that day. (e) If the subliminal message always took place on certain days, for example, on weekends, that could be a confounding variable. It would not be clear if observed higher popcorn sales were due to the subliminal messages or to the weekend. Random assignment of days for subliminal messages is a control over this variable. (f) Compare the quantity of popcorn bought by the treatment group—that is, by the people who receive the subliminal message—to the quantity bought by the control group, which is the people who don’t receive the message. This is a well-designed experiment incorporating comparison, replication, random assignment, and control. So if a difference is noted, a cause- and-effect conclusion is justified.

questions.stem: A six-month study looked at 800 adult volunteers who were randomly divided into four groups. ■The first group wore a clip-on fitness tracker and received a cash incentive if they walked more than 50,000 steps a week. ■The next group also wore an activity tracker and received a cash incentive for walking more than 50,000 steps a week. However, they were required to donate the cash to charity. ■A third group wore the activity tracker but did not receive a cash incentive. ■The last group did not wear a fitness tracker or get a cash incentive. The measured outcome was “change in blood pressure over a six- month period.” (a) Was this an observational study or an experiment? Explain. (b) Identify the treatments, experimental units, and response variable. (c) What is the fourth group called, and what is the purpose of including it? (d) Describe an appropriate method for assigning the subjects to the four groups so that each group will have an equal number of subjects. (e) Is it reasonable to generalize the results of the study beyond the 800 participants? Explain why or why not.
questions.answer_text: (a) This was an experiment because treatments, which involved fitness trackers and incentives, were applied. (b) Treatments: (1) tracker and personal cash incentive, (2) tracker and charity cash incentive, (3) tracker alone, and (4) no tracker or cash incentive. Experimental units: the 800 volunteers. Response variable: change in blood pressure over a six-month period. (c) The “no fitness tracker or incentive” group was a control group whose purpose is to provide a baseline to determine if the activity tracker or cash incentive treatments had any effect on blood pressure change. (d) Assign each participant an integer from 1 to 800. Use a random integer generator to choose 600 unique integers between 1 and 800, throwing away repeats. The participants corresponding to the first 200 of these selected integers will be put in the first group, the participants corresponding to the second 200 of these selected integers will be put in the second group, the participants corresponding to the last 200 of these selected integers will be put in the third group, and the remaining 200 participants will be put into the fourth group. (e) These 800 participants were volunteers, who may not be representative of a larger population with regard to the effects of wearing fitness trackers or receiving cash incentives on changes in blood pressure. So it is not reasonable to generalize the results of this study to a larger population.

questions.stem: Some diseases have developed resistance to medications that were once commonly used to treat them. A dermatologist conducted an experiment on a form of chronic eczema that had become increasingly difficult to treat. From a sample of 20 teenagers with the disease, he treated 10 with a new calcineurin inhibitor for 5 days and treated the remaining people with a standard treatment of topical corticosteroids for 5 days. He had all 20 teenagers rate their itch intensity on a scale of 0 to 10 before and after their respective treatments. What were the experimental units of this study?
questions.answer_text: The experimental units are the people who participated in the study.

questions.stem: A new strain of flower is being tested for THC content. Fifty flowers of the strain are randomly assigned to be analyzed when either dried or fresh. Which of the following would provide the best evidence that the average THC content of the flower is different when dried or fresh?

This would provide convincing evidence that the average THC content of the flower is different when dried or fresh.

questions.stem: An experiment was conducted to investigate whether teenagers can stand longer on one foot with their eyes open or closed. Thirty students from a teacher’s math classes volunteered to participate. Drawing names out of a hat resulted in two groups of equal size, one to stand with eyes open and the other with eyes closed. The mean number of seconds volunteers could stand on one foot with their eyes closed was calculated to be shorter than with eyes open. Which of the following elements of a well-designed experiment is missing? I. Random assignment of treatments to experimental units II. Comparison of at least two treatment groups III. Replication
questions.answer_text: Picking names out of a hat gives random assignment. There was a comparison of the two treatments, standing with eyes open or with eyes closed, and there were 15 subjects in each treatment group. Note that replication refers to having more than one experimental unit in treatment groups, not to repeating the experiment multiple times.

questions.stem: A game designer plans to test whether any of three different background music genres leads to improved game enjoyment. Sixty gamers who actively play Minecraft volunteer for the study and will be randomly assigned to 3 groups of 20 volunteers each. Three musical genres will be randomly assigned to be piped in through headphones to the volunteers so that each group of 20 volunteers receive a different genre for 1 hour while playing Minecraft. Before and after the session, everyone rates their enjoyment of playing Minecraft, and changes are recorded. Why is this considered to be a completely randomized design?
questions.answer_text: The treatments, which are the three musical genres piped into the headphones, will be randomly assigned to the volunteers.

questions.stem: A study was conducted to evaluate the effectiveness of a topical cream for relief of arthritis. Sixteen volunteers suffering from moderate arthritis rubbed the cream on painful joints for 10 days. Twelve of the volunteers reported some pain relief. The company concluded that the topical cream was more effective than no treatment for moderate arthritis 75% of the time. Which of the following best explains why the company’s conclusion is not supported by this study?
questions.answer_text: Using volunteers makes it difficult to generalize to a population. However, the main problem here is the lack of a control group. Without a control group, there could well have been confounding variables, including the placebo effect.

questions.answer_text: The experiment is to determine the effect of having a parent sitting beside a child, and clearly a child will know if a parent is beside him or her.

questions.stem: A study is conducted to determine which of two seamstresses can sew a better dress. They each sew a dress using their own pattern, material, and sewing machine. Both seamstresses then use the same questionnaire passed out to a random sample of their customers who view and evaluate their final product. Answers on the questionnaires were then compared. Which of the following is not true about this study?
questions.answer_text: Combining two different populations each possibly subject to several confounding variables will not allow generalizing to any population.

options.A: The reported 1470 result is an average; there could have been a wide spread of exam scores for students using either of the review books.
options.B: The student probably used the review book for the other group either intentionally or by mistake.

options.D: This indicates a confounding variable in the original experiment.

questions.stem: A school is trying to evaluate two SAT prep review books. Two- hundred twenty of the school’s students are signed up to take the SAT exam in 2 months. The school randomly assigns 110 of these students to receive a free copy of one of the review books and gives the other 110 students a free copy of the other review book. After the exam, the school notes that the students given the first review book averaged 1470 for the combined SAT score, while those given the second review book averaged 1250. Based on this, the school orders copies of the first review book for all of its students planning to take the next SAT exam. One of those students ends up scoring 1255. Which of the following is the best explanation of the difference between that student’s score and the score reported in the study for those using that review book?
questions.answer_text: The students using the first review book average 1470 on the SAT exam. This says nothing about the spread of exam scores among the 110 students using the book. The spread could be dramatic with nothing unusual about a single score of 1255.

options.B: The choices of sugar, oil, flour, and chips

questions.stem: In search for the perfect chocolate chip cookie, 16 separate batches were prepared using white or brown sugar, butter or vegetable oil, all-purpose or bread flour, and semisweet or milk chocolate chips. Each of the batches was divided into three parts, with the three parts randomly assigned to be baked immediately, chilled for 1 hour before baking, or chilled for 24 hours before baking. The cookies were then judged on a 1 to 10 scale as to whether they were chewy and soft with a crisp exterior. What were the treatments in this experiment?
questions.answer_text: What is being manipulated on all the preparations is whether they are baked immediately, chilled for 1 hour before baking, or chilled for 24 hours before baking.

options.A: Students in each block should be as similar as possible, for example, similar IQ scores.
options.B: Students in each block should be as different as possible, for example, different IQ scores.
options.C: Students should be randomly assigned to the blocks.
options.D: Students in the same block should receive the same teaching method.

questions.stem: A randomized block design tests the effect of three teaching methods on student performance. Which of the following should guide the formation of blocks?
questions.answer_text: In a randomized block design, the subjects are grouped into blocks based on similar characteristics and then randomly assigned treatments within each block. For example, the researchers in this example might want to test the three different teaching methods separately on students with high IQs, on students with average IQs, and on students with low IQs.

questions.stem: A medical researcher plans to test a new medication to improve focus and reduce impulsivity in teens with ADHD (attention deficit hyperactivity disorder). The researcher has recruited 25 pairs of teens, each pair with the same age, same gender, same ADHD diagnosis (inattentive, hyperactive-impulsive, or combined), and same severity of symptoms. Each teen will receive either the new medication or a placebo for 1 month. At the end of the month, each teen will be evaluated as to lessening of symptoms. (a) Identify the treatments, experimental units, and response variable. (b) Describe a statistical advantage of using a matched pairs design rather than using a completely randomized design. (c) Describe how the treatments can be randomly assigned using a matched pairs design.
questions.answer_text: (a) Treatments: New medication, placebo Experimental units: 50 teens with ADHD Response variable: Lessening of ADHD symptoms (b) Pairing similar teens (same age, same gender, same ADHD diagnosis, and same severity of symptoms) allows for variation in ADHD symptoms due to the new medication, which could be distinguished from the listed common variables. This would not be possible in a completely randomized experiment. By using the matched pairs design, the difference in symptom lessening between the new medication and a placebo is easier to measure. It is easier to find convincing evidence that the new medication is better than a placebo. (c) Label each pair of similar teens as A and B. For each pair, toss a coin. If heads, teen A gets the new medication and teen B gets the placebo. If tails, teen B gets the new medication and teen A gets the placebo.

questions.stem: A bike-riding school teaches children to ride on bikes with training wheels before teaching them to ride on bikes without training wheels. A study was conducted with 25 children to determine if first using a balance bike (remove the pedals) before using training wheels would be quicker. Each of 15 children participating in the study first trained on a balance bike for 1 lesson followed by using training wheels until they could ride without the training wheels. Each of the other 10 children participating in the study first trained on a balance bike for 2 lessons followed by using training wheels until they could ride without the training wheels. (a) Was this an observational study or an experiment? Explain. (b) When the study ended, it was clear that first training on a balance bike for 2 lessons followed by using training wheels was more successful than training on a balance bike for 1 lesson followed by using training wheels. Would the researchers be justified in saying that first training on a balance bike for 2 lessons followed by using training wheels is a quicker method of learning to ride a bike than just using lessons with training wheels? Explain. (c) Does it matter how the 25 children were separated into the two groups? Explain.
questions.answer_text: (a) This was an experiment because two treatments were applied: 1 lesson followed by using training wheels and 2 lessons followed by using training wheels. (b) No, they would not be justified. The experiment did not compare 2 lessons followed by using training wheels with just using lessons with training wheels. (c) It would be important to use random assignment for the two groups. For example, if all the older children were put in one of the groups, then age would have been a confounding variable.

questions.stem: For each of the following, would you recommend using random sampling, random assignment, both, or neither? Explain. (a) A teacher wants to investigate whether the promise of bonus points or a chocolate chip cookie motivates students to study more for a test. (b) A sports statistician wants to investigate whether a greater proportion of high school students would rather attend a football game or a basketball game. (c) A student wants to know if the average age of administrators is greater than the average age of teachers at her school.
questions.answer_text: (a) It is important for the teacher to use random assignment for choosing which students are offered bonus points and which are offered a chocolate chip cookie because a cause-and-effect conclusion is of interest. (b) This cannot be random assignment because you don’t want to assign students to go to a game. Instead, you want to know their preferences. However, it would be good to use random sampling to increase the chance of getting a representative sample and being able to generalize to the whole population. (c) The student would probably want to interview all the administrators and teachers at the school. So neither sampling method is appropriate.

questions.stem: There is a pressure point on the wrist that some doctors believe can be used to help control the nausea experienced following certain medical procedures. The idea is to place a band containing a small marble firmly on a patient’s wrist so that the marble is located directly over the pressure point. A certain procedure involves a 2-day hospital stay because of severe nausea complications. A doctor plans to test the correct pressure point placement versus an improper marble placement on 50 patients. He will use a matched pair test where each patient is a block. Each day, patients will rate their nausea level on a scale of 1 to 10. (a) Identify the explanatory variable in this study and classify it as categorical or quantitative. (b) Identify the response variable in this study and classify it as categorical or quantitative. (c) Is this a prospective observational study, a retrospective observational study, or an experiment? Explain. (d) Should blinding be incorporated? Explain. (e) Should random sampling or random assignment be incorporated? Explain how. (f) Why is it important for there to be some kind of control with regard to which days the correct pressure point is used? (g) In context, explain how a cause-and-effect conclusion will or will not be justified. USE CORRECT TERMINOLOGY! Bias: when a study systematically favors certain outcomes Blinding: refers to subjects not knowing which treatment they are receiving Block design: an experimental design where subjects are divided into representative groups to bring certain differences into the picture and reduce variation (for example, blocking by gender, age, or race) and randomization then takes place within each block Census: an attempt to include the entire population Cluster random sample: involves dividing the population into heterogeneous groups called clusters and then picking everyone in a random sample of the clusters Completely randomized design: an experimental design in which everyone has an equal chance of receiving any treatment Confounding: when there is uncertainty as to which variable is causing an effect Control group: a group given no treatment or a sham treatment Double-blinding: refers to subjects and those evaluating their responses not knowing who received which treatments Experimental study: involves applying a treatment to one or more groups and observing the responses
questions.answer_text: (a) The explanatory variable is the correct or improper placing of the marble. This is a categorical variable. (b) The response variable is self-reported nausea level. This is a numerical variable as it is on a 1 to 10 scale. (c) This is an experiment with two treatments: correct and improper placement of a marble to a pressure point. (d) Yes, blinding should be incorporated because of a possible placebo effect. If patients knew they were receiving the correct marble placement, they might psychologically feel less nauseous even if the marble was ineffective. Similarly, if patients knew they were receiving the improper marble placement, they might psychologically feel more nausea than expected. (e) Random assignment should be incorporated. Each patient is a block and so should receive both treatments, one each of the two days, randomly chosen. For example, number the patients 1 to 50. Use a random number generator to pick integers between 1 and 50, throwing out repeats, until 25 unique integers are picked. The patients with numbers corresponding to the 25 picked integers should receive correct marble placement the first day, while the remaining 25 patients should receive correct marble placement the second day. (f) For example, nausea levels might naturally be less on the second day. If all the patients received the correct pressure point placement on the second day and seemed to feel relief, it would be unclear whether the marble or the day was the cause of the relief. Marble and day would be confounded. This variable is controlled by the random assignment of treatments to days. (g) This is a well-designed experiment incorporating comparison, replication, random assignment, and control. So if patients rate nausea relief differently depending upon correct or improper placement of the marble, a cause-and-effect conclusion is justified.

questions.answer_text: No. In a normal distribution the mean and median should be equal or nearly equal, but here the mean, 6.4, is significantly greater than the median, 5. (d) With a larger sample size, the sampling distribution of x̅ will be even closer to a normal distribution and will have a tighter clustering (a smaller standard deviation). questions.stem: In a random sample of 500 American women between the ages of 45 and 64, 305 said that breast cancer was the medical condition they feared most. questions.answer_text: (a) Parameter: Let p represent the proportion of the population of American women between the ages of 45 and 64 who would say that breast cancer is the medical condition they fear most. For independence, we are given that this is a random sample, and clearly 500 is less than 10% of all American women between the ages of 45 and 64. For normality, np̂ = 305 ≥ 10 and n(1 − p̂ ) = 195 ≥ 10. Mechanics: Calculator software gives (0.554, 0.666). [For instructional purposes, we note that or (0.554, 0.666).] Conclusion in context: We are 99% confident that the true proportion of all American women between the ages of 45 and 64 who would say that breast cancer is the medical condition they most fear is between 0.554 and 0.666. (b) If all possible random samples of 500 women between the ages of 45 and 64 were surveyed, we would expect about 99% of the resulting confidence intervals to contain the true proportion of all American women between the ages of 45 and 64 who would say that breast cancer is the medical condition they fear most. questions.answer_text: The p-value is a conditional probability; in this case, there is a 0.032 probability of an observed difference in sample proportions as extreme as (or more extreme than) the one obtained if the null hypothesis is assumed to be true.

questions.stem: Cyberbullying is a growing problem, and for those who suffer cyberbullying, the effects can be devastating. Which of the following is the most reasonable conclusion for the company’s hypothesis at the α = 0.05 significance level?
questions.answer_text: The 99% confidence interval does not contain 0. questions.stem: In a random sample of 500 new births in the United States, 41.2% were to unmarried women, while in a random sample of 400 new births in the United Kingdom, 46.5% were to unmarried women. (a) Calculate a 95% confidence interval for the difference in the proportions of new births to unmarried women in the United States and the United Kingdom. (b) Does the confidence interval support the belief by a UN health care statistician that the proportions of new births to unmarried women is different in the United States and the United Kingdom? Explain.
questions.answer_text: (a) Parameters: Let pUS represent the proportion of the population of new births in the United States that are to unmarried women. Let pUK represent the proportion of the population of new births in the United Kingdom that are to unmarried women. Procedure: Two-sample z-interval for a difference between population proportions, pUS − pUK, the difference in population proportions of new births to unmarried women in the United States and the United Kingdom. Checks: We are given these are random samples, they are clearly independent, and the sample sizes, 500 and 400, are less than 10% of new births in the United States and the United Kingdom, respectively. For normality, nUS p̂ US = (500)(0.412) = 206 ≥ 10, nUS (1 − p̂ US) = (500)(0.588) = 294 ≥ 10, nUK p̂ UK = (400)(0.465) = 186 ≥ 10, and nUK (1 − p̂ UK) = (400) (0.535) = 214 ≥ 10. Mechanics: Calculator software (such as 2-PropZInt on the TI-84) gives (−0.1182, 0.01219). [For instructional purposes, we note that: Conclusion in context: We are 95% confident that the true difference in proportions, pUS − pUK, of new births to unmarried women in the United States and the United Kingdom is between −0.118 and 0.012. (b) Because 0 is in the interval of plausible values for the difference of population proportions, this confidence interval does not support the belief by the UN health care statistician that the true proportions of new births to unmarried women are different in the United States and the United Kingdom.

questions.stem: A national survey before the death of Ruth Bader Ginsburg studied whether or not a random sample of American voters could name a single Supreme Court justice. The study compared survey responses between voters under the age of 35 and voters over the age of 65. The following table displays some of the results. Difference Voters under Voters over (percentage All Voters 35 65 points) Number 2,050 1,500 550 surveyed % who could 54% 57% 46% 11% not name a justice (a) Is random sampling, random assignment, both, or neither involved in this study? Explain. (b) What are the appropriate hypotheses for testing whether the two populations of voters differ with regard to the proportion who cannot name a single Supreme Court justice? (c) The test statistic is z = 4.43. What does this value mean in context? (d) Is there convincing evidence to reject the null hypothesis at the 0.01 significance level? Explain. (e) A 99% confidence interval based on these data is (0.04612, 0.17388). Interpret this interval in context. (f) Is this confidence interval consistent with the test decision in part (d)? Explain.
questions.answer_text: (a) The sample was said to be selected randomly. There was no random assignment into ages or into who answered with what response. (b) H0: p35 = p65 and Ha: p35 ≠ p65, where p35 is the proportion of all voters under age 35 who cannot name a single Supreme Court justice, and p65 is the proportion of all voters over age 65 who cannot name a single Supreme Court justice. (c) The two sample proportions (voters under 35 and over 65 who cannot name a single Supreme Court justice) are 4.43 standard deviations (or standard errors) apart. (d) With this large of a z-score, 4.43, the p-value will be very small, so there is sufficient evidence to reject the null hypothesis. That is, there is convincing evidence that the proportion of all voters under 35 years old who cannot name a single Supreme Court justice is different from the proportion of all voters over 65 years old who cannot name a single Supreme Court justice. (e) We are 99% confident that the proportion of all voters under age 35 who cannot name a single Supreme Court justice is greater than the proportion of all voters over age 65 who cannot name a single Supreme Court justice by between 0.04612 and 0.17388. (f) Since the confidence interval contains only positive values—that is, does not include zero as a plausible value for the difference in population proportions—the two procedures give consistent results.

questions.stem: A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial across the United States and parts of Canada tested hydroxychloroquine as a postexposure prophylaxis for asymptomatic participants reporting a high-risk exposure to a confirmed Covid-19 contact. The incidence of Covid-19 among participants receiving hydroxychloroquine was 49 out of 414, while the incidence among participants receiving a placebo was 58 out of 407. (a) Explain the purpose of random assignment in this experiment. (b) State the hypotheses the researchers tested about hydroxychloroquine use as a postexposure prophylaxis for Covid-19. (c) Identify the hypothesis test the researchers used to analyze the results of this experiment and show that the conditions for this test were met. (d) The p-value of this test is 0.152. What conclusion should be made at the α = 0.05 significance level? (e) What error might have been committed, Type I or Type II, and what would be a possible consequence?
questions.answer_text: (a) The purpose of random assignment is to create two groups of subjects that are roughly equivalent except for the treatment, hydroxychloroquine or placebo, received. This allows for a cause-and-effect conclusion about hydroxychloroquine and a lowered susceptibility to Covid-19 if the difference between the two groups is statistically significant. (b) H0: phydro = pplacebo and Ha: phydro < pplacebo, where phydro is the true probability of contracting Covid-19 after taking hydroxychloroquine as a postexposure prophylaxis for asymptomatic participants reporting a high-risk exposure to a confirmed Covid-19 contact, and pplacebo is the true probability of contracting Covid-19 after taking a placebo for asymptomatic participants reporting a high-risk exposure to a confirmed Covid-19 contact. (c) Two-sample z-test for a difference of two population proportions. ■The treatments were randomly assigned. , we have nhydro p̂ c = (414)(0.130) = 53.8, nhydro (1 − p̂ c) = (414) ■With (0.870) = 360.2, nplacebo p̂ c = (407)(0.130) = 52.9, and nhydro (1 − p̂ c) = (414)(0.870) = 360.2 are all at least 10. (d) With this large of a p-value, 0.152 > 0.05, there is not sufficient evidence to reject the null hypothesis; that is, there is not convincing evidence that hydroxychloroquine is any better than a placebo for preventing Covid-19 when used as a postexposure prophylaxis for asymptomatic participants reporting a high-risk exposure to a confirmed Covid-19 contact. (e) There was not convincing evidence to reject the null hypothesis, so a Type II error might have been committed—that is, failing to reject a false null hypothesis. If so, the researchers would not have recommended using hydroxychloroquine as a postexposure prophylaxis for asymptomatic participants reporting a high-risk exposure to a confirmed Covid-19 contact when, in reality, hydroxychloroquine is effective and should have been recommended.
